claims.text: capacity-plan.md inputs: 1,000 shops (from multi-shop-requirements.md, itself an assumption), 50 orders/shop/day, busiest day x2, 12% of a day's orders in its busiest hour, 40 product reads per placed order; every input after shops is marked (giả định).

Results: 50,000 orders/ordinary day, 100,000 busiest day; ~0.6 orders/s average vs ~3.3/s (12,000 in one hour) at peak; ~23 vs ~133 product reads/s; the plan uses the busiest hour because the average is over five times lower.

Ceiling per process by Little's law: max throughput = 20 / time per read; lab read time with 20 permits full ~10-12 ms (lab number, assumption), so ~20/0.012 ≈ 1,600 reads/s per process; 2 api Pods ≈ 3,200.

catalog-reads lets 20 product reads run and 5 wait per process (PermitLimit = 20, QueueLimit = 5), so the load test saw 503 only beyond 25; the ASP.NET Core concurrency limiter counts in one process's memory, so each api Pod has its own 20 permits.
claims.source_hint: DonHang.Api/Program.cs lines 143-148, 162-166 @ stage-4; ASP.NET Core docs, Rate limiting middleware, Concurrency limiter

claims.text: Base api.yaml: replicas: 2, one api process per Pod, no podAntiAffinity or topologySpreadConstraints; production overlay patches replicas to 3. The plan counts 2 without giving a reason and does not size for one node running both Pods.

Headroom rule: peak under half the ceiling of the 2 api Pods so one Pod carries all if the other is lost; the lesson states it as all Pods but one. Product reads 133 vs ~1,600: passes; orders 3.3/s, one short transaction each: passes.

Runs out first: if Redis stops or the DB slows and a read takes 200 ms, ceiling per process is 100/s, half the ceiling of 2 Pods is 100 < 133, so catalog-reads runs out first and returns 503 for product reads while orders still run.

Steps in order: (1) add api Pods, each adds 20 read permits and one connection pool, so Pod count is bounded by max_connections; (2) move the product list to the replica when its peak crosses the primary's headroom.

Each api Pod keeps one Npgsql pool for ConnectionStrings:Default at default size (connection string sets none); Payments, Notifications, migrations and the backup job connect to the same server; read max_connections with SHOW, not guessed.
Npgsql keeps a connection pool per connection string inside each process; its default Maximum Pool Size is 100. So 6 Pods with default pools could ask PostgreSQL for up to 600 connections.
claims.source_hint: Npgsql docs, Connection String Parameters: Pooling, Maximum Pool Size

claims.text: PostgreSQL accepts at most max_connections; once active connections reach max_connections minus superuser_reserved_connections (and reserved_connections), only superusers are accepted. Read the value with SHOW max_connections.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL 17 docs, 19.3.1 Connection Settings (max_connections, superuser_reserved_connections); SQL command SHOW

claims.text: A Pod whose resource requests fit no node is not scheduled and stays Pending.
claims.source_hint: Kubernetes docs, Resource Management for Pods and Containers: how Pods with resource requests are scheduled

claims.text: Triggers for a new plan: shops or average orders per shop off by more than a quarter; one shop over 10% of the busiest day's orders; Program.cs changes a limit, api.yaml changes Pod count, or staging read time differs far from the lab's.
Plan from the busiest hour, not the daily average, when sizing a rate the system must answer, because a shared resource runs out while load is highest and the average hides that hour.

Trade-offs: daily average hides the peak; busiest-hour plan with marked assumptions needs triggers; biggest server pays for unmeasured capacity and leaves catalog-reads permits and max_connections unchanged; more Pods need node room and add pools.
claims.source_hint: reasoning from capacity-plan.md and Program.cs lines 143-148 @ stage-4

claims.text: Worked arithmetic (not repo numbers): 50 ms read -> 20/0.05 = 400/s per process, half of 2 Pods = 400 > 133; 2,000 shops and 100 ms -> peak ~267, 200/s per process, half of 2 Pods = 200 < 267; with 3 Pods, losing one leaves 400 > 267.
A one-shop limit keeping a busy shop from slowing others is a later lesson (backend.l4.per-shop-limits); moving the product list to the replica is backend.l4.read-routing.

A Deployment with no strategy uses RollingUpdate with maxUnavailable 25% (rounded down) and maxSurge 25% (rounded up); with 2 replicas that is 0 and 1, so a third Pod starts before an old one stops; so a release does not leave one Pod alone.
claims.source_hint: Kubernetes docs, Deployments: Rolling Update Deployment, Max Unavailable and Max Surge
